rules.rule: Every vowel is pure and clear
rules.explain: A=ah, E=eh, I=ee, O=oh, U=oo. CIAO = chow. Sing each vowel fully — never swallow them!

rules.rule: C and G change before E/I
rules.explain: CA=ka but CE=che, CI=chee. GA=ga but GE=je. CH forces KA (CHIESA=kee-EH-sa), GH forces GA.
FAMIGLIA = fah-MEE-lyah (family). LASAGNA = lah-ZAHN-ya. GN hums like onion's NI!
PALA (shovel) vs PALLA (ball) — hold the L! ANNO (year) stretches the N. Double = longer, always.
GRA-zie, PI-zza, GE-la-to. An accent mark forces final stress: CITTÀ (city), CAFFÈ (coffee).

alphabet.title: The Italian alphabet: 21 letters
alphabet.explain: Italian uses 21 letters — J K W X Y appear only in foreign words. Learn names to spell aloud: MI CHIAMO … (my name is …), SI SCRIVE … (it is spelled …).

letters.tip: S, or Z between vowels: CASA

counting.title: Counting 0 to 100
counting.explain: Learn 0–10 by heart. 11–19 glue together (undici, diciotto). 20+ joins tens + ones and DROPS a vowel: ventuno (not ventiuno!). 100 = CENTO.
rules: 11–16 glue: undici (11), sedici (16). 17–19 double up: diciassette.

lessons.title: Ciao! Greetings and politeness
lessons.learn: CIAO fits friends (hello AND bye!). Strangers get BUONGIORNO (daytime) and BUONASERA (evening). Leaving: ARRIVEDERCI. Magic trio: PER FAVORE (please), GRAZIE (thanks), SCUSI (sorry).

grammar.title: Articles: IL/LO/LA + UN/UNO/UNA
grammar.explain: Masculine: IL libro, but LO before s+consonant/z (LO zaino). Feminine: LA casa. A/AN: UN libro, UNO zaino, UNA casa. Learn nouns WITH articles!
mistakes: Saying IL zaino — s/z words take LO/UNO: LO zaino.
Saying LA libro — libro is masculine: IL libro.

lessons.title: Numbers and introductions
lessons.learn: Numbers 1–10 open prices and ages. Introduce with ESSERE (to be): SONO = I am. Sono Sofia. Ask names: COME TI CHIAMI? (What are you called?). Answer: MI CHIAMO …

grammar.title: ESSERE: sono, sei, è
grammar.explain: SONO = I am, SEI = you are, È = he/she is. Drop the pronoun: SONO Sofia is enough! È wears an accent (è) — never confuse with E (and)!
mistakes: Saying E (and) for È (is) — is needs the accent: È!
Saying IO SONO every time — SONO alone is natural.

lessons.title: Tu o Lei: scegliere alla prima frase
lessons.learn: Italian decides before it says anything else: tu for friends and family, Lei for strangers, shops and anyone older. Buongiorno opens both doors; the pronoun picks the room.

grammar.title: The two yous
grammar.pattern: tu + 2nd person singular · Lei + 3rd person singular · scusi (Lei) / scusa (tu)
grammar.explain: Buongiorno signora, come sta? Buongiorno Marco, come stai? Lei takes the verb of lui — sta, not stai — which is the whole trick of polite Italian.

examples.en: Good morning madam, how are you?
Excuse me, are you the teacher?

mistakes.why: Lei takes the third-person verb form: sta.
With Lei the excuse is scusi, not scusa.

dialogue.t: Buongiorno, scusi, Lei è il professor Bianchi?
dialogue.r: bwohn-JOR-noh, SKOO-zee, lay eh eel proh-fes-SOR BYAHN-kee?
dialogue.en: Good morning, excuse me, are you Professor Bianchi?
My name is Sofia. I'm new.

lessons.title: Family and AVERE (age)
lessons.learn: Meet the family: MADRE, PADRE, FRATELLO, SORELLA. Age uses AVERE (to have): HO 10 ANNI = I have 10 years = I am 10. Ask: QUANTI ANNI HAI? (How many years do you have?)

grammar.title: AVERE for age: ho… anni
grammar.explain: HO = I have, HAI = you have, HA = he/she has. Age: HO + number + ANNI. QUANTI ANNI HAI? = How old are you? (H is silent: HO = oh!)
mistakes: Saying SONO dieci anni — age always uses AVERE.
Pronouncing the H in HO — silent! HO = oh.

lessons.title: Food and -ARE verbs
lessons.learn: Food first! ACQUA, PANE, LATTE, MELA. Order with VORREI (I would like): VORREI UN CAFFÈ. -ARE verbs: PARLARE → PARLO (I speak), PARLI (you speak), PARLA (he/she speaks).

grammar.title: Present -ARE: parlo, parli, parla
grammar.explain: Drop -ARE, add -O (I), -I (you), -A (he/she). PARLARE → parlo, parli, parla. MANGIARE → mangio, mangi, mangia. One pattern, hundreds of verbs!
mistakes: Saying TU PARLA for 'you speak' — you = PARLI.

lessons.title: Dove abito: c'è, ci sono
lessons.learn: Home is described with C'È (there is) and CI SONO (there are) plus a room list: un appartamento, una camera, la cucina, il soggiorno.

grammar.title: There is / there are
grammar.pattern: c'è + singular · ci sono + plural · abito + place
grammar.explain: C'è una cucina e ci sono due camere. In camera non c'è il balcone. The negative swaps the article for nothing: non c'è balcone.

mistakes.why: One room takes c'è; ci sono is plural.

grammar.title: Four endings: -o/-a/-i/-e
grammar.explain: ROSSO (m), ROSSA (f), ROSSI (m plural), ROSSE (f plural). -E adjectives (verde, grande): VERDE → VERDI (plural both genders). BLU never changes!

lessons.title: Days, months, and telling time
lessons.learn: Days are lowercase except with capitals? No — Italian days are LOWERCASE: lunedì, martedì. Time: CHE ORE SONO? È L'UNA (1:00) but SONO LE TRE (others). Half: E MEZZA.

grammar.title: Telling time: è l'una / sono le…
grammar.explain: È L'UNA (1:00 — singular), SONO LE DUE/TRE… (plural). Half: E MEZZA — SONO LE TRE E MEZZA (3:30). Quarter: E UN QUARTO.
grammar.pattern: è l'una · sono le + number (+ e mezza)
mistakes: Saying SONO L'UNA — one o'clock is È L'UNA.
Capitalising days (Lunedì) — Italian days are lowercase.

lessons.title: Il tempo e le stagioni
lessons.learn: Weather is impersonal and short: FA BEL TEMPO, PIOVE, FA FREDDO. Seasons take IN for the ones you live through: in estate, in inverno.

grammar.title: Weather frame
grammar.pattern: fa + adjective · piove / nevica · in estate / in inverno
grammar.explain: In estate fa bel tempo e la gente esce. In inverno fa freddo e a volte nevica. Notice that weather uses fare: fa caldo, fa freddo, fa bel tempo.

examples.en: In summer the weather is nice.

examples.t: In inverno fa freddo e nevica.
examples.r: een een-VEHR-noh fah FRED-doh eh NEH-vee-kah.
examples.en: In winter it is cold and it snows.

dialogue.en: The weather is nice and everyone goes out. It's the best season.

items.q: Say aloud: Vorrei un caffè, per favore.

culture.text: Ciao is for friends and family; with a stranger, a shopkeeper or anyone older, Italian opens with buongiorno and closes with arrivederci. The tu/Lei decision is made in the first sentence — tu for people you would call by first name, Lei for everyone else, including anyone whose surname you know.

reading.text: Sofia arriva al bar la mattina. « Buongiorno, un caffè, per favore. » Il barista risponde: « Buongiorno! Desidera altro? » Lei prende un cornetto e chiede l'ora. « Sono le otto e un quarto. » Dice grazie e arrivederci, poi va al lavoro a piedi, perché l'ufficio è qui vicino.
reading.gloss: Sofia arrives at the bar in the morning. 'Good morning, a coffee, please.' The barista answers: 'Good morning! Would you like anything else?' She takes a croissant and asks the time. 'It is a quarter past eight.' She says thank you and goodbye, then walks to work, because the office is nearby.

listening.script:
Sofia: Buongiorno, come sta?
Marco: Bene, grazie. E Lei?
Sofia: Bene. Come si chiama, scusi?
Marco: Marco. Piacere!
listening.gloss: Sofia: Good morning, how are you? Marco: Fine, thanks. And you? Sofia: Fine. What is your name, excuse me? Marco: Marco. Pleased to meet you!

idioms.literal: until we see each other again

mistakes.right: Buongiorno, come sta? / Ciao, come stai?
mistakes.why: Ciao and the polite Lei form cannot share a sentence.
Grazie takes no object; to insist, say grazie mille.

task.title: Meet someone twice
task.instructions: Write the same introduction twice: once at a party to someone your age (tu, first name) and once at a doctor's reception (Lei, surname). Keep both to four lines and read them aloud — the politeness lives in the pronoun and the verb ending, not in the adjectives.
